newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa tires easily but joins prayers.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa tires easily but joins prayers.

text.p: CALCUTTA, India, Sept 14 (Reuter) Nobel peace prize winner Mother Teresa, released from hospital last week, is attending morning prayer services but grows exhausted quickly and spends most of her time resting in bed, her aides said on Saturday.
"Though she is much better than before, she is not all right," said a spokeswoman for Missionaries of Charity, the religious order the Albanian-born Roman Catholic nun founded.
"She enquires about our work and attends only morning services, that too on a wheel chair. But she gets exhausted quickly."
The 86-year-old nun, who won the Nobel prize in 1979 for her work helping the poor, was admitted to a hospital on August 20 with malaria and pneumonia. She later developed cardiac problems.
The nun, sometimes called the "Saint of the Gutters" for her work among the destitute, was released from hospital on September 6.
"She is still very weak and needs complete bed rest for a couple of months," her personal cardiologist, Dr. A. K. Bardhan, told Reuters on Saturday.
"Her cardiac irregularity is still there and she was given oxygen support on a few occasions after her release from the hospital," Bardhan said.
The spokeswoman said the nun was not in a position to attend any major events and spent most of her time resting in bed.
"She talks with us and smiles sometimes. But we don't go to her room much because we don't want to disturb her, she said.

Last week, in her first speech after release from the hospital and the 50th anniversary of her calling, Mother Teresa urged nuns in her religious order to rededicate themselves to the cause of the poor.
The order she founded in 1949 runs around 300 homes for unwanted children and the destitute in India and abroad.

Mother Teresa's health began to deteriorate in 1989, when she was fitted with a heart pacemaker. A year later, the Vatican announced she was stepping down as Superior of her Missionaries of Charity order.
She was asked to stay on after more than 100 delegates from all over the world could not agree on a successor.
The nun was treated for heart disease in California in 1991. In 1993 she fell in Rome and broke three ribs and developed malaria later that year.
